<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par137 />{{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=10|verse=18}}. A still further weakening of the ''indefinite'' use of {{GHGheb|text=מָה}} is the combination {{GHGheb|text=מַה־שֶּׁ·|translate=that which}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=1|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=3|verse=15|hidebook=1}} (just like the Syriac {{GHGheb|text=מָא דְ}}); cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=8|verse=1}}, and {{GHGheb|text=בַּל... מָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=9|verse=13}}, {{GHGheb|text=לֹא... מָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=2|verse=12}}, ''nothing whatever''.—On {{GHGheb|text=מְא֫וּמָה|translate=quicquam}}, ''anything at all'' (usually with a negative), and as an adverb ''in any way'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=21|verse=3}}, see the Lexicon.<section end=par137 />

<section begin=par138 />{{GHGpar-heading|138|The Relative Pronoun}}

<div style="font-size: small; text-align: center;">Cf. Philippi, ''Stat. constr.'' (see heading of § 89), p. 71 f., and especially V. Baumann, {{GHGcite|title=Hebräische Relativsätze}}, Leipzig, 1894.</div>

{{GHGmargin-letter|138|a}}
Relative clauses are most frequently (but not necessarily; cf. {{GHGpar|155|b}}) introduced by the indeclinable {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} (see § 36).<ref>The etymology of the word is still a matter of dispute. Against the identification of {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}, as an original substantive, with the Arabic ''ʾaṯar'', ''trace'', Aram. {{GHGheb|text=אֲתַר|translate=place, trace}}, Nöldeke urges ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xl. 738) that the expression ''trace of''... could hardly have developed into the relative conjunction, while the meaning of ''place'' has been evolved only in Aramaic, where the word is never used as a relative. According to others, {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} is really a compound of several pronominal roots; cf. Sperling, ''Die Nota relationis im Hebräischen'', Leipzig, 1876, and König, {{GHGcite|title=Lehrgeb.}}, ii. 323 ff., who follows Ewald and Böttcher in referring it to an original {{GHGheb|text=אֲשַׁל}}. According to Hommel ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xxxii. 708 ff.) {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} is an original substantive, to be distinguished from {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ·}} and {{GHGheb|text=שַׁ·}} (an original pronominal stem), but used in Hebrew as a ''nota relationis'', or (as {{GHGheb|text=זֶה}} and {{GHGheb|text=זוּ}} are also sometimes used, see below, ''g'' and ''h'') simply for the ''relative pronoun''. Baumann (op. cit., p. 44) sees in the Assyrian ''ša'', Phoenician, Punic, and Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ}}, the ground-forms, of which the Phoenician and Punic {{GHGheb|text=אש}} (see above, § 36 note) and the Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} are developments.</ref> This is not, however, a relative pronoun in the Greek, Latin, or English sense, nor is it a mere ''nota relationis'',<ref>E.g. like Luther’s use of ''so'', in ''die fremden Götter, so unter euch sind'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=35|verse=2}}.</ref> but an original ''demonstrative'' pronoun [as though ''iste, istius'', &c.].<ref>This is the necessary conclusion both from the analogy of the Arabic ''ʾallaḏi'', which is clearly a demonstrative (like the Hebr. {{GHGheb|text=הַלָּז}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַלָּזֶה}}), and from the use of {{GHGheb|text=זֶה}} and {{GHGheb|text=זוּ}} as relatives.</ref> Hence it is used—

(1) In immediate dependence on the substantival idea to be defined, and virtually in the same case as it (hence belonging syntactically to the main clause); e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=7}}... {{GHGheb|text=יְהֹוָה אֲשֶׁר לְקָחַ֫נִי... הוּא יִשְׁלַח|translate=the Lord, iste, he took me}}... ''he shall send'', &c. (= ''who took me''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=2}} ''and God finished'' {{GHGheb|text=מְלַאכְתּוֹ אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה|translate=his work, istud, he had made}} (it). Such qualifying clauses may be called ''dependent relative clauses''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|138|b}}
Rem. 1. In the above examples {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=7}} is virtually in the nominative, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=2}} in the accusative. A further distinction between the examples is that in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=7}} the main idea ({{GHGheb|text=יהוה}}), to which {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} is added in apposition, is only resumed in the qualifying clause by the subject (''he'') inherent in<section end=par138 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>
